 The picture for silver by the CoT: update
 By  Jonathan Da Silva 
 Published: Nov 17, 2026 - 3:54 PM Updated: Nov 17, 2026 - 4:13 PM Kitco Commentaries Opinions, Ideas and Markets Talk 
 Featuring views and opinions written by market professionals, not staff journalists.
 (Kitco Commentary) - In my last piece I wrote about the gradual rebuilding of managed money short positions in silver after they had collapsed to historically low levels earlier this year. At the time, the question was straightforward: would the shorts keep coming back, and would silver eventually stop responding to the added bearish pressure?
 I have updated the table below with one change. Rather than comparing positioning with the monthly high in silver , I am using the monthly low. If we are looking for a contrarian bottom here, the low is the more useful reference point: it shows how much bearish positioning is being built as price is being pushed lower.
 October finished with managed money gross shorts peaking at 13,543 contracts, up from 9,272 in September. 
 It's possible that the short side was simply waiting to see whether the bulls could reclaim and hold $50; they couldn't. A technical failure followed by lower prices gives trend-following traders a much cleaner reason to press the short side, and from a contrarian standpoint, I would actually like to see that happen. Even at 13,567 contracts, managed money shorts remain nowhere near the 25,000-plus levels seen through much of 2023, let alone the extreme of 41,987 contracts reached in February 2024. The bearish trade is rebuilding, but it is not crowded yet, in my opinion.
 I think the next sign to watch for is a meaningful increase in managed money shorts following the failed $50 reclaim. The more important signal comes after that: shorts continue to build, but silver stops making materially lower lows - or begins rising anyway.
 Good luck.
 Jonathan Da Silva 
 Jonathan Da Silva developed a passion for hard money and economics from a young age having been influenced by family who sought to teach me that "nothing is free", and the importance of intrinsic value early on.
